summary: Give the Hohmann transfer calculator the mass of primary body, the radius of primary body, the gravitational constant and the altitude and it returns gravitational parameter. It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Hohmann transfer calculator work?
sections.html:
The Hohmann transfer calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports gravitational parameter in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the mass of primary body, the radius of primary body, the gravitational constant (G) and the altitude (Initial orbit).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hohmann transfer calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Gravitational parameter=(1 ÷ 100000000000) × gravitational constant (G) × mass of primary body
Initial orbit radius=altitude + radius of primary body
Initial orbit radius=(specific angular momentum ^ 2) ÷ gravitational parameter
Initial orbit radius=specific angular momentum ÷ velocity at point "p"
Altitude=destination orbit radius − radius of primary body
Specific angular momentum=the square root of (destination orbit radius × gravitational parameter)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Mass, opening in masses of the Earth
  • Volume, opening in cubic kilometers
  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Viscosity – kinematic, opening in square kilometers per second
  • Speed, opening in kilometers per second
  • Length, opening in kilometers

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Hohmann transfer calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the mass of primary body, the radius of primary body and the gravitational constant — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Hohmann transfer calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns gravitational parameter, derived from the mass of primary body, the radius of primary body and the gravitational constant. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Hohmann transfer calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the mass of primary body, the radius of primary body, the gravitational constant and the altitude, which is 8 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter mass of primary body in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Mass of primary body opens in masses of the Earth and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Hohmann transfer calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
